subject.title: To a Child Dancing upon the Shore
subject.author: William Butler Yeats
subject.text:
Dance there upon the shore;
       What need have you to care
       For wind or water's roar?
       And tumble out your hair
       That the salt drops have wet;
       Being young you have not known
       The fool's triumph, nor yet
       Love lost as soon as won.
       And he, the best warrior, dead
       And all the sheaves to bind! .
       What need that you should dread
       The monstrous crying of wind?
                              William Butler Yeats

              FALLEN MAJESTY
Although crowds gathered once if she but showed her face
And even old men's eyes grew dim, this hand alone,
Like some last courtier at a gipsy camping place

title: He Wrote Her a Warning, Then Became One
standfirst: In August 1912 Yeats watched Maud Gonne's eighteen-year-old daughter dance on a Normandy beach and wrote her a poem cataloguing every grief that adulthood would bring her. Five years later, in a London teashop, he turned out to be one of them.

sections.heading: Dusk at Les Mouettes
sections.body:
At dusk in August 1912, on the beach below Les Mouettes, the Gonne family's villa on the Normandy coast at [Colleville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colleville-sur-Mer), an eighteen-year-old girl danced barefoot at the edge of the tide. William Butler Yeats, forty-seven and a summer guest of the household, watched her, and that same month wrote her a poem — later placed, in his next collection, directly after another poem he was drafting on the same visit, "The Mountain Tomb."

The dancer was [Iseult Gonne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iseult_Gonne), daughter of Maud Gonne — the woman Yeats had loved, and been refused by, for more than twenty years — and the French journalist Lucien Millevoye. Maud passed her off to the wider world as an adopted niece; inside the household Iseult was not permitted to call her mother "mother" and used "Moura" instead. Nor was this the first marriage proposal to have passed between Yeats and this particular child. Some years earlier — fifteen, by one biographer's account; fourteen, by another's — Iseult had asked Yeats to marry her, in a joking way, and been turned down on the grounds, as he put it, that there was too much Mars in her horoscope.

The poem he wrote her that August was published four months later in Chicago, in Harriet Monroe's *Poetry* magazine, under the title "To a Child Dancing upon the Shore." On the printed page it runs straight into the next poem below it, Yeats's own "Fallen Majesty," about a beauty whose face once made even old men's eyes grow dim — a juxtaposition owed to the typesetter, not the poet, but a strange one to land on all the same.

sections.heading: From Warrior to Labourer
sections.body:
At twelve lines, the poem makes a single argument: the child dancing has not yet met the griefs waiting for grown men and women, so she has no cause to dread the wind. Yeats lists those griefs like a summons she hasn't reached yet — the fool's triumph, love lost as soon as won, and, in the text *Poetry* printed in December 1912, a dying figure he called that year "the best warrior": "And he, the best warrior, dead / And all the sheaves to bind!"

He changed his mind about that line. When he collected the poem two years later in *Responsibilities* (1914), retitled "To a Child Dancing in the Wind," the dead man was no longer a warrior. The revised text reads "Nor the best labourer dead / And all the sheaves to bind" — a reaper, not a soldier, his harvest left standing in the field. It is a quieter image than the one it replaced, and an odder one to find in a poem about a girl on a beach: not a death that ends a cause, but one that simply stops a job half finished.

sections.heading: Two Years Later, Twelve Lines On
sections.body:
Yeats did not let the poem stand alone. In *Responsibilities* he numbered it "I" and ran a second poem straight after it as "II": "Two Years Later." Where the first poem is confident enough to ask what the dancer has to fear, the second admits it never actually told her:

> Has no one said those daring
> Kind eyes should be more learn'd?
> Or warned you how despairing
> The moths are when they are burned?
> I could have warned you; but you are young,
> So we speak a different tongue.

It ends by handing her the very fate the first poem had only gestured at — "Suffer as your mother suffered, / Be as broken in the end" — and repeating, with the blame quietly reversed, its own excuse for having said nothing: "But I am old and you are young, / And I speak a barbarous tongue."

Scholars disagree about when this second poem was actually written. [A. Norman Jeffares](https://revistas.usp.br/abei/en/article/download/184198/170567), who spent years editing Iseult's own letters, dates it to "December 1912 or 1913." [Amanda French](https://amandafrench.net/files/IseultGonne.pdf), writing in the *Yeats Eliot Review*, places its composition in 1914, tying it to the year Iseult broke her foot in three places and, warned by a specialist that an unrested fracture would leave her "lame for life," ignored the advice anyway. Either dating makes much the same point: whatever the title's two years had actually contained, they had already given the poet something to be right about.

sections.heading: The Proposal at the Teashop
sections.body:
Five years after the beach poem was drafted, Yeats went back to Colleville and, having already asked Maud's permission the previous summer, proposed to Iseult himself. It was 1917; she was twenty-three. By Jeffares's account he proposed to her "repeatedly throughout the summer" without getting a clear answer either way. That September the party — Yeats, Maud, Iseult, her half-brother Seán — sailed together for England, and on the crossing Yeats gave Iseult an ultimatum: marry him, or he would ask someone else. They arranged to settle it at an ABC teashop in London. She refused him there. Two months later, on 20 October 1917, Yeats married [Georgie Hyde-Lees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertha_Georgie_Yeats).

He told Lady Gregory that "poor Iseult was very depressed on the journey" and had gone off by herself at Le Havre to cry, ashamed, she said, at being so selfish as not to want to marry him and so end their friendship — an account her future husband, Francis Stuart, later disputed, recalling that she told the story herself "in a tone of banter." Of his own motives, Yeats never settled on one version. Writing about the courtship, he offered this: "[I have not I think been in love with Iseult](https://therumpus.net/2012/05/19/saturday-history-lesson-the-unrequited-yeats/) — I have been nearly mad with pity." It reads like a rewrite, five years on, of the same warning the beach poem had given her — except that this time the poet was the thing she needed warning about.

sections.heading: Three Explanations and One Coincidence
sections.body:
Yeats's biographers have never agreed on why, once Maud Gonne had refused him for what both of them by then understood to be the last time, he turned to her daughter. Harold Bloom called it "the poet's brief, strange, quasi-love for Iseult Gonne." Joseph Hone thought it more practical: "It was Iseult's prospects that now most afflicted his thoughts... He was more heart-smitten than he quite realised." Richard Ellmann thought it was mostly about Yeats: "Marriage seemed the solution to many problems: it would give him a family, a home, and peace of mind in which to work." The writer Monk Gibbon put the arrangement more plainly than any of them, noting that a man who had loved the mother and then wanted, years later, to marry the daughter "has almost the tang of a Maupassant story."

Whichever explanation is right, the dates keep one grim appointment on their own. Amanda French's account of Iseult's life closes on it directly: she died in March 1954, aged fifty-nine, of heart disease diagnosed, French writes, "in the same summer Yeats published 'To a Child Dancing in the Wind'" — the same revision, that is, in which a dying warrior became a dying labourer, his sheaves left lying in the field unbound.
